b.v: Zeno of Elea, a follower of the philosopher Parmenides, devised paradoxes meant to show that motion is impossible. In one, swift Achilles can never overtake a tortoise that has a head start, because each time he reaches the point where the tortoise was, it has moved a little farther ahead. For centuries many readers ______ such paradoxes as clever wordplay; only with the nineteenth-century theory of limits did mathematicians give a rigorous account of how infinitely many shrinking distances can add up to a finite one.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: relished
dismissed
authenticated
reconciled

b.v: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle describes each virtue as a mean between two vices: courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness. The mean, however, is not a fixed midpoint that can be calculated in advance. It is, Aristotle insists, relative to the person and the circumstances, and finding it requires practical wisdom developed through experience—a view that makes his ethics less ______ than a rulebook and more like a skill to be practiced.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: persuasive
ambiguous
mechanical
subjective

b.v: Born around 870 near Farab, a town on the Syr Darya in what is now Kazakhstan, Abu Nasr al-Farabi wrote commentaries on Aristotle so influential that later scholars called him “the Second Teacher,” second only to Aristotle himself. ⟦Al-Farabi was more than a transmitter of Greek thought, however: in The Virtuous City, he described an ideal state led by a philosopher-ruler whose wisdom guides its citizens toward happiness, joining ideas from Plato’s Republic to Islamic views of prophecy.⟧

q.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
o: It provides evidence that al-Farabi’s title of “the Second Teacher” was undeserved.
It explains how al-Farabi’s birthplace influenced his political philosophy.
It contrasts al-Farabi’s political views with Aristotle’s views on ethics.
It qualifies the description in the previous sentence by showing that al-Farabi also developed ideas of his own.

b.v: Text 1

In An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), David Hume observed that when one billiard ball strikes another, we see only that the motion of the second ball follows the impact of the first. We never perceive any “necessary connection” between cause and effect; our expectation that the second event must follow arises from habit, formed by repeated experience.
Text 2

Immanuel Kant later wrote that reading Hume interrupted his “dogmatic slumber.” But Kant did not accept Hume’s conclusion. In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), he argued that the concept of cause is not derived from experience at all: it is one of the concepts the mind itself supplies, without which no coherent experience of events would be possible.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would Kant (Text 2) most likely respond to Hume’s explanation (Text 1) of why people expect one event to follow another?
o: He would accept that experience never reveals such a necessity but would deny that the concept of cause is merely a product of habit.
He would reject Hume’s claim that we observe one event following another.
He would argue that repeated experience is the only reliable source of the concept of cause.
He would agree with Hume’s explanation but add that habit is one of the concepts the mind supplies.

b.v: Epictetus, a Stoic philosopher of the first and second centuries CE, was born into slavery in Hierapolis and later taught in Nicopolis, in Greece. He wrote nothing himself; his student Arrian recorded his lectures and compiled the Enchiridion, or Handbook. Its opening lines divide all things into those within our power—our judgments, desires, and aversions—and those outside it, such as our bodies, property, and reputation. Epictetus held that we are disturbed not by events but by our judgments about them, so freedom lies in governing the first category and accepting the second.

q.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Epictetus’s early life in slavery was the main source of his philosophy.
Arrian changed Epictetus’s lectures to emphasize ideas about property and reputation.
In teachings preserved by a student, Epictetus located human freedom in governing one’s own judgments rather than external circumstances.
Stoic philosophers taught that people should try to gain control over their bodies and reputations.

b.v: Walden (1854) recounts the two years that Henry David Thoreau spent living in a small cabin he built near Walden Pond in Massachusetts. Thoreau presents his time at the pond as a deliberate experiment, undertaken to discover what a life reduced to its essentials could teach him: ______

q.s: Which quotation from Walden most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.”
“I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach.”
“Our life is frittered away by detail.”
“Simplify, simplify.”

b.v: In 1967 the philosopher Philippa Foot introduced the thought experiment now known as the trolley problem, which Judith Jarvis Thomson later extended. In one version, a person can pull a lever to divert a runaway trolley so that it kills one person instead of five; in another, the only way to save the five is to push a large man off a footbridge into the trolley’s path. Some psychologists hypothesize that people’s moral judgments in such cases depend less on the number of lives saved than on whether the harm is caused by direct physical force.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologists’ hypothesis?
o: Most participants would save five people rather than one in every version of the problem.
Participants respond more slowly to versions of the problem that involve larger numbers of people.
Participants who have studied philosophy approve of pulling the lever more often than other participants do.
Most participants who approve of pulling the lever to save five people disapprove of pushing the man off the footbridge to save the same five.

b.v: According to Plutarch, the Athenians preserved the ship of Theseus for centuries by replacing each rotting plank with new timber, and philosophers argued over whether it remained the same ship. In the seventeenth century, Thomas Hobbes sharpened the puzzle: suppose someone had collected the discarded planks and reassembled them into a second ship. If a ship’s identity depends on the continuity of its form and use, the repaired ship in the harbor is the ship of Theseus; if it depends on its original material, the reassembled ship is. Hobbes’s version of the puzzle thus suggests that ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: two criteria of identity that each seem reasonable on their own can single out different objects.
the Athenians should not have replaced the ship’s planks.
objects made of wood cannot keep their identity over time.
the identity of an object depends on its original material rather than on continuity.

b.v: Ibn Rushd—known in Latin Europe as ______ commentaries on Aristotle so thorough that the theologian Thomas Aquinas referred to him simply as “the Commentator.”

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: Averroes, wrote
Averroes wrote
Averroes—wrote
Averroes; wrote

b.v: Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949), in which she argues that “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,” ______ translated into dozens of languages and remains a founding text of modern feminist philosophy.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: have been
has been
were
being

b.v: Socrates left no writings of his own; what we know of his thought comes mainly from his students, above all Plato, whose dialogues usually make Socrates their main speaker. ______ scholars face a lasting difficulty: separating the views of the historical Socrates from the views that Plato may have placed in his teacher’s mouth.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: Nevertheless,
Similarly,
For instance,
Consequently,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: Abai Kunanbayuly (1845–1904) was a Kazakh poet, composer, and thinker.
His Book of Words is a collection of 45 short prose pieces.
Each piece is called a “word.”
In them, he reflects on education, work, morality, and the future of the Kazakh people.
He also translated poems by Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Lermontov into Kazakh.

q.s: The student wants to describe the form of the Book of Words to an audience unfamiliar with Abai. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Abai Kunanbayuly, a Kazakh poet, composer, and thinker, lived from 1845 to 1904.
Abai translated poems by Pushkin and Lermontov into Kazakh, in addition to writing the Book of Words.
The Book of Words, by the Kazakh thinker Abai Kunanbayuly (1845–1904), is a collection of 45 short prose pieces, each called a “word.”
In the Book of Words, Abai reflects on education, work, morality, and the future of the Kazakh people.

b.v: Once the fourth-largest lake in the world, the Aral Sea began to ______ in the 1960s, after Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton fields in Central Asia; by the late 1980s, it had split into two separate bodies of water.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: dwindle
proliferate
ossify
meander

b.v: The shrinking of the Aral Sea is often cited as one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century. ⟦In 2005, however, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral Dam, which separated the northern part of the sea from the southern part; within a few years the northern sea’s water level had risen, fish had returned, and a local fishing industry had begun to revive.⟧ The larger southern part, most of which lies in Uzbekistan, continued to shrink.

q.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
o: It explains why the Aral Sea began to shrink in the twentieth century.
It argues that the shrinking of the Aral Sea was less severe than commonly believed.
It presents a partial recovery that contrasts with the broader decline described in the text.
It describes a project that reversed the shrinking of both parts of the sea.

b.v: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the world’s deepest lake and holds roughly a fifth of the unfrozen fresh water on Earth’s surface. Yet a lake’s surface area can be a poor guide to how much water it contains: ______

q.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
o: Lake Superior has the greatest surface area of the lakes in the table and also holds the greatest volume of water.
Lake Victoria has a greater surface area than Lake Tanganyika and a much smaller maximum depth.
Lake Baikal reaches a maximum depth of 1,642 meters, the greatest of any lake in the table.
Lake Baikal has less than half the surface area of Lake Superior but holds nearly twice as much water.

b.v: Text 1

In 1973 the German historian Arno Peters presented a world map that he called a fairer alternative to the Mercator projection. Mercator’s map, published in 1569, keeps compass directions accurate, which made it invaluable to navigators, but it greatly enlarges regions far from the equator: Greenland appears about as large as Africa, although Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. Peters argued that his equal-area map finally showed the world’s regions at their true relative sizes.
Text 2

Many cartographers objected less to Peters’s goal than to his claims. The projection he promoted had already been described by the Scottish clergyman James Gall in 1855, and it achieves equal areas only by stretching and squashing the shapes of continents. Because no flat map can preserve both area and shape, these critics argued, every projection is a compromise, suited to some purposes and not to others.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would the cartographers in Text 2 most likely respond to Peters’s argument in Text 1?
o: By rejecting Peters’s claim that the Mercator projection distorts the sizes of regions far from the equator.
By granting that his map shows relative areas accurately while disputing that it is either original or free of serious distortion.
By arguing that the Mercator projection remains the best map for most purposes because it keeps compass directions accurate.
By claiming that Gall’s map distorted the shapes of continents less than Peters’s map did.

b.v: Some weather stations in Chile’s Atacama Desert have recorded no measurable rain for years at a time. The desert is caught between two barriers to moisture. To the east, the Andes block humid air moving from the Amazon basin. To the west, the cold Humboldt Current chills the air above the Pacific Ocean, creating a temperature inversion—a layer of warm air above cooler air—that keeps rain clouds from forming. Parts of the desert are so dry and lifeless that NASA has used the region to test instruments designed to search for life on Mars.

q.s: According to the text, why does so little rain fall in the Atacama Desert?
o: Cold ocean water cools the air near the coast, producing conditions that keep rain clouds from forming, while mountains block moist air from the east.
The Andes prevent moist air from the Pacific Ocean from reaching the desert.
Its soil, which resembles that of Mars, absorbs moisture before rain can fall.
Instruments tested by NASA have shown that the air above the desert contains no water.

b.v: The nerpa, or Baikal seal, is the only seal species that lives exclusively in fresh water, and it is found only in Russia’s Lake Baikal, far from any ocean. How seals reached the lake is still debated. Genetic studies show that the nerpa’s closest relatives are the ringed seal of the Arctic Ocean and the Caspian seal, rather than seals of warmer southern seas. Taken together with the fact that the Angara, the only river flowing out of Baikal, joins the Yenisei, which empties into the Arctic Ocean, these findings suggest that ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: the nerpa evolved in Lake Baikal from a freshwater species that has since died out elsewhere.
the ringed seal descended from nerpas that left Lake Baikal by way of the Angara River.
seals that live in fresh water are most likely to be found in lakes connected to the Caspian Sea.
the ancestors of the nerpa most likely reached Baikal from the Arctic by way of river systems rather than from a southern sea.

b.v: By most measurements, the Nile is the world’s longest river, about 6,650 kilometers in ______ some researchers who trace the Amazon to a more distant source in the Peruvian Andes argue that the Amazon is longer still.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: length, however,
length; however,
length however,
length however

b.v: Each of the fourteen mountains on Earth that rise more than 8,000 meters above sea level ______ in Asia, in either the Himalaya or the Karakoram range.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: lie
are lying
lies
have lain

b.v: Kazakhstan, which covers about 2.7 million square kilometers, is the largest landlocked country in the world: none of its territory touches the open ocean. ______ the country has a long coastline on the Caspian Sea, a body of water large enough to support ports such as Aktau.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: Even so,
Therefore,
In other words,
Similarly,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: Mount Everest’s summit is 8,849 meters above sea level, the highest on Earth.
This height was announced in 2020 after a joint survey by China and Nepal.
Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises 4,207 meters above sea level.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea is more than 10,000 meters tall.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth’s surface farthest from Earth’s center.

q.s: The student wants to emphasize that which mountain counts as the “tallest” depends on how height is measured. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Mount Everest, whose height of 8,849 meters was announced in 2020, is the highest mountain on Earth.
China and Nepal conducted a joint survey of Mount Everest, announcing in 2020 that its summit is 8,849 meters above sea level.
Mauna Kea rises 4,207 meters above sea level, but measured from the ocean floor it is more than 10,000 meters tall.
Everest has the highest summit above sea level, but Mauna Kea is taller from base to summit, and Chimborazo’s summit is farthest from Earth’s center.

b.v: Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, is often described as the coldest national capital in the world, with January nights that can fall below −30°C. A climatologist argues that the city’s harsh winters result less from its latitude than from its location deep in the interior of Asia, far from the moderating influence of the ocean, and from its elevation of about 1,350 meters.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the climatologist’s argument?
o: Ulaanbaatar is located farther north than most of Mongolia’s other large towns.
Ulaanbaatar’s summers are fairly warm, with July temperatures that often rise above 20°C.
Paris, which lies at nearly the same latitude as Ulaanbaatar but at low elevation and near the Atlantic Ocean, has much milder winters.
Mongolia has a smaller population than most other countries in Asia.

b.v: In 1997 Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to the city now called Astana. Officials pointed to several drawbacks of the old capital, including its ______ earthquakes and the limited room for growth in its location at the foot of the Zailiysky Alatau mountains.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: indifference to
susceptibility to
resistance to
contribution to

b.c: Rotation and Orbit of the Inner Planets
rows: Time to orbit the Sun once (Earth days)

b.v: A planet’s rotation period is the time it takes to spin once on its axis, and its orbital period is the time it takes to circle the Sun once. On Earth the first is far shorter than the second, and it is tempting to assume that the same holds for every planet. The data show otherwise: ______

q.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
o: Mars rotates in about the same time as Earth does but takes nearly twice as long to orbit the Sun.
Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun.
Mercury takes about 58.6 Earth days to rotate once and about 88 Earth days to orbit the Sun.
Earth has the shortest rotation period of the four planets in the table.

b.v: In 1847, the Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis found that when doctors in his Vienna clinic washed their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. Many of his colleagues nonetheless ______ his conclusions, in part because no accepted theory explained how invisible matter on a doctor’s hands could cause disease; only after the germ theory advanced by Louis Pasteur and others did his insight gain wide acceptance.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: replicated
anticipated
embellished
rebuffed

b.v: When Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known chemical elements into his periodic table in 1869, he left gaps for elements that no one had yet found and soon predicted their properties. In 1875 the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium, which matched one of these predictions—except that he measured its density as 4.7 grams per cubic centimeter, well below the 5.9 Mendeleev had predicted. Mendeleev wrote that the sample was probably impure. When Lecoq de Boisbaudran purified the metal and measured it again, he obtained a density of about 5.9.

q.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a prediction, presents a result that seemed to contradict it, and explains how further work resolved the apparent contradiction.
It compares two scientists’ competing theories and explains why one of them was eventually rejected.
It summarizes a discovery and then argues that its importance has been exaggerated.
It describes a failed prediction and then explains how the theory was revised to account for it.

b.v: Text 1

In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass, which later broke apart and drifted to their present positions. He pointed to the way the coastlines of South America and Africa seem to fit together and to fossils of the same species, such as the small aquatic reptile Mesosaurus, found on both continents.
Text 2

Most geologists of Wegener’s time rejected continental drift. Their main objection was not to his evidence, which many found intriguing, but to his inability to explain what force could push enormous continents through the solid crust beneath the oceans. Only in the 1960s, when studies of the seafloor showed that new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward, did geologists gain a mechanism that made the movement of continents plausible.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely characterize the evidence described in Text 1?
o: As misleading, since the similarity of fossils on separate continents has a simpler explanation.
As decisive, since it should have convinced geologists even without an explanation of its cause.
As suggestive but insufficient to win acceptance without a plausible mechanism for the movement of continents.
As irrelevant to the later discovery that new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges.

b.v: Tardigrades, microscopic animals often called water bears, can survive conditions that would kill almost any other animal. When their surroundings dry out, they lose nearly all the water in their bodies, curl into a shape called a tun, and slow their metabolism almost to a stop; in this state, some have revived after years. In 2007, tardigrades carried into orbit on the European Space Agency’s FOTON-M3 mission survived exposure to the vacuum of space, and some even survived additional exposure to intense ultraviolet radiation.

q.s: According to the text, what enables tardigrades to survive when their surroundings dry out?
o: They store extra water in a protective shell called a tun.
They move to nearby places where water is still available.
Exposure to radiation strengthens them against drying out.
They enter a dormant state in which they lose most of their water and their metabolism nearly stops.

b.v: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold contaminating one of his culture plates had killed the Staphylococcus bacteria around it. He named the active substance penicillin but could not produce it in a stable, purified form, and for about a decade it attracted little attention. At the University of Oxford, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain then developed methods to purify penicillin and showed in the early 1940s that it could cure bacterial infections. When the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Fleming, Florey, and Chain, the decision implied that the committee considered ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: Fleming’s discovery to have been accidental and therefore less deserving of recognition.
the work of turning a laboratory observation into a usable medicine to be a contribution comparable to the original discovery.
the purification of penicillin to have been impossible without Fleming’s direct help.
penicillin to be less important than other discoveries made in the 1940s.

b.v: Marie Curie remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different ______ physics, which she shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel in 1903, and chemistry, which she received alone in 1911.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: sciences;
sciences,
sciences:
sciences

b.v: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin, Voyager 2, the probe ______ a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth, intended for any intelligent beings who might one day find it.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: carries
carry
are carrying
have carried

b.v: Light travels about 300,000 kilometers per second, yet sunlight still needs roughly eight minutes to cross the 150 million kilometers between the Sun and Earth. ______ when we look at the Sun, we see it not as it is at that moment but as it was about eight minutes earlier.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: Nevertheless,
By contrast,
Similarly,
As a result,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: CRISPR-Cas9 is a tool that scientists use to edit genes.
It can cut DNA at a precise, chosen location.
The tool was adapted from a natural defense system that bacteria use against viruses.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna described the gene-editing method in 2012.
They received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for this work.

q.s: The student wants to explain the natural origin of the CRISPR-Cas9 tool. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on CRISPR-Cas9.
CRISPR-Cas9, a tool for editing genes, was adapted from a natural defense system that bacteria use against viruses.
CRISPR-Cas9 can cut DNA at a precise, chosen location.
In 2012, Charpentier and Doudna described a method of gene editing.

b.v: On the small Galápagos island of Daphne Major, the biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant measured hundreds of medium ground finches year after year. During a severe drought in 1977, the small, soft seeds the birds usually eat became scarce, leaving mostly large, hard seeds. Many finches died, and the survivors tended to have deeper beaks. The Grants concluded that the drought had produced evolutionary change in the population, not merely the deaths of some individuals.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the Grants’ conclusion?
o: Beak depth is largely inherited, and birds hatched after the drought had deeper beaks on average than the population before the drought.
Some finches with shallow beaks also survived the drought.
Finches on other Galápagos islands have beaks of many different shapes.
The number of seeds on Daphne Major returned to normal after the drought ended.

b.v: On the Origin of Species (1859) was attacked by critics who saw in it a bleak, purposeless picture of nature. Charles Darwin himself, however, presented the process he described as a source of wonder: ______

q.s: Which quotation from On the Origin of Species most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “I have called this principle, by which each slight variation, if useful, is preserved, by the term of Natural Selection.”
“Multiply, vary, let the strongest live and the weakest die.”
“There is grandeur in this view of life… from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.”
“We see nothing of these slow changes in progress, until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages.”

b.v: Found by French soldiers in 1799, the Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because scholars could already read the Greek, the stone gave them a ______ for deciphering the hieroglyphs, though more than two decades passed before Jean-François Champollion announced his breakthrough in 1822.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: pretext
deterrent
foothold
substitute

b.v: For more than a millennium, a web of overland and sea routes connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean. The name usually given to this network, however, is modern: the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coined the term Seidenstrasse, or “Silk Road,” in 1877. ⟦In fact, few merchants traveled the whole distance; goods passed from trader to trader through cities such as Samarkand and Otrar, and silk was only one commodity among many, alongside horses, spices, glass, and paper—as well as religions, including Buddhism.⟧

q.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
o: It complicates the picture of trade suggested by the name discussed in the previous sentence.
It explains why Richthofen chose to name the routes after silk.
It argues that silk was the most valuable commodity carried along the routes.
It describes how Buddhism first reached Samarkand and Otrar.

b.v: Text 1

In essays written in the 1930s, the linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf argued that the language a person speaks shapes how that person thinks. His best-known example was the Hopi language, which, he claimed, contains no words or grammatical forms that treat time as a flowing quantity, so that its speakers must conceive of time differently from speakers of European languages.
Text 2

In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a detailed study documenting that Hopi does in fact have many expressions for units and sequences of time, undermining Whorf’s most famous claim. Yet weaker versions of Whorf’s idea have found support. In a 2007 experiment, for example, Russian speakers, whose language has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, distinguished between those shades slightly faster than English speakers did.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Whorf’s view as described in Text 1?
o: By arguing that Malotki’s study confirms Whorf’s claims about the Hopi language.
By claiming that language has no measurable effect on how people perceive the world.
By suggesting that the differences between Russian and English are greater than Whorf predicted.
By rejecting his evidence about Hopi while allowing that language may have modest effects on how people perceive the world.

b.v: Completed in 537 under the Byzantine emperor Justinian, Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was for nearly a thousand years the largest cathedral in the world. After the Ottoman conquest of the city in 1453, it was converted into a mosque, and minarets were added around it. In 1934 the government of the Turkish Republic turned it into a museum, a decision that reflected the secular ideals of the new state, and in 2020 it was reclassified as a mosque. Few buildings record so clearly the political changes of the city around them.

q.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years.
The changing uses of Hagia Sophia over many centuries reflect the shifting political history of its city.
The Ottomans added minarets to Hagia Sophia to mark its conversion into a mosque.
The Turkish Republic’s decision of 1934 was reversed because the building was too large to serve as a museum.

b.v: “‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers” is a poem written around 1861 by Emily Dickinson. In the poem, the speaker suggests that hope sustains people without demanding anything from them in return: ______

q.s: Which quotation from “‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers” most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers - / That perches in the soul -”
“And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -”
“Yet - never - in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of me.”
“And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -”

b.v: In 1952 the architect Michael Ventris showed that Linear B, a script found on clay tablets in Crete and mainland Greece, had been used to write an early form of Greek. Linear B developed from an older Cretan script, Linear A, and many of their signs look nearly identical. Scholars have therefore been able to assign approximate sound values to many Linear A signs and to pronounce many of its words, yet the meaning of those words remains largely unknown. This situation suggests that ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: the main obstacle to reading Linear A lies in the unknown language it records rather than in the script itself.
Ventris’s decipherment of Linear B was based on mistaken sound values.
Linear A was used to write an early form of Greek older than the one recorded in Linear B.
the signs of Linear A changed so much over time that they cannot be compared with those of Linear B.

b.v: More than 7,000 pages of Leonardo da Vinci’s notebooks survive, and most of them share a peculiar feature: they are written in mirror ______ Leonardo wrote from right to left, with each letter reversed, so that his notes are most easily read in a mirror.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: script,
script
script: and
script;

b.v: The Terracotta Army, which farmers digging a well near the city of Xi’an discovered in 1974, ______ of thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried with Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: consist
consists
consisting
have consisted

b.v: The Bible that Johannes Gutenberg printed in Mainz in the 1450s is often described as the first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type. ______ movable metal type itself was not a European invention: in Korea, a Buddhist text known as the Jikji had been printed with movable metal type in 1377.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: For example,
Therefore,
However,
Likewise,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: Esperanto is a constructed language.
It was created by L. L. Zamenhof, an eye doctor in Warsaw.
Zamenhof published the first book describing the language in 1887.
He hoped it would serve as an easy-to-learn second language for international communication.
The name comes from Zamenhof’s pen name, Doktoro Esperanto, meaning “one who hopes.”

q.s: The student wants to explain the purpose for which Esperanto was created. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: L. L. Zamenhof created Esperanto in the hope that it would serve as an easy-to-learn second language for international communication.
Esperanto takes its name from Doktoro Esperanto, the pen name of its creator, meaning “one who hopes.”
In 1887, L. L. Zamenhof published the first book describing Esperanto.
Esperanto, a constructed language, was created by an eye doctor in Warsaw.

b.v: After Johann Sebastian Bach died in 1750, his music fell out of fashion, and for decades his large choral works were rarely performed. Many music historians credit the twenty-year-old Felix Mendelssohn’s 1829 performance of Bach’s St Matthew Passion in Berlin with sparking a broad revival of interest in the composer.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians’ claim?
o: Mozart and Beethoven studied some of Bach’s keyboard works in the decades after his death.
The St Matthew Passion was first performed in Leipzig in 1727.
Mendelssohn’s performance used a smaller choir and orchestra than Bach’s original performances did.
Public performances and new editions of Bach’s works increased sharply in the years immediately following 1829.

b.v: In Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, a painting long attributed to Pieter Bruegel the Elder, the climax of the myth seems almost ______: Icarus appears only as a pair of legs vanishing into the sea in a corner of the canvas, while in the foreground a ploughman goes on working, apparently unaware of the boy’s fall.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: ornate
incidental
triumphant
prophetic

b.v: In Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter (1850), set in seventeenth-century Puritan Boston, Hester Prynne is sentenced to wear a scarlet letter A on her dress as a mark of shame. Hester, however, embroiders the letter with an elaborate border of gold thread, so that the badge meant to humiliate her becomes strikingly beautiful. In this way, Hawthorne allows his heroine to ______ the punishment’s intended meaning, turning a public [[indignity|V08-indignity]] into a display of her own skill and pride.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[extol|V01-extol]]
[[subvert|V05-subvert]]
[[corroborate|V07-corroborate]]
[[codify|V12-codify]]

b.v: When Herman Melville died in 1891, he was remembered chiefly, if at all, as the author of Typee (1846), an early adventure book set in the South Seas. Moby-Dick (1851) had sold poorly, and many reviewers had found it baffling. Interest in the novel revived only in the 1920s, after the scholar Raymond Weaver published a biography of Melville in 1921. Today Moby-Dick is so firmly ______ that it is hard to imagine a course on American literature without it.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[canonical|V07-canonical]]
[[innocuous|V07-innocuous]]
[[sporadic|V11-sporadic]]
[[obsolete|V02-obsolete]]

b.v: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself appeared in 1845, seven years after Douglass escaped from slavery in Maryland. Some readers at the time doubted that a formerly enslaved man could have written so eloquent a book, and the words “Written by Himself” in the title answered them directly. ⟦Douglass also named the men who had enslaved him and the places where he had lived, details that readers could check but that exposed him to the risk of recapture.⟧ Soon after the book appeared, he left for a speaking tour of Britain and Ireland, where he remained for nearly two years.

q.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
o: It explains why Douglass chose to publish his book outside the United States.
It provides evidence that the readers who doubted Douglass had underestimated his talent as a speaker.
It describes a reaction to the book that its author had not anticipated.
It describes a choice that helped [[substantiate|V01-substantiate]] the book’s account while putting its author in danger.

b.v: Text 1

Ernest Hemingway wrote in 1935 that “all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn.” Yet Hemingway, like many later critics, judged the novel’s last chapters a failure. In them, Tom Sawyer stages an elaborate, playful scheme to free Jim, a man who has escaped from slavery and been captured, although Tom knows all along that Jim has already been freed in his owner’s will. To these critics, the ending turns Jim’s struggle for freedom into a game and [[squanders|V09-squander]] the moral seriousness of the novel’s best chapters.
Text 2

Other scholars read the ending differently. Twain wrote it in the early 1880s, as the promises of Reconstruction were being abandoned across the South. On this reading, the absurdity of Tom’s scheme is deliberate: Jim, free [[de jure|V03-de_jure]] but still held captive and treated as a plaything, mirrors the situation of Black Americans who had been freed by law but were still denied liberty in practice.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would the scholars in Text 2 most likely respond to the critics’ judgment in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that the ending is a failure but blaming it on the pressures of publishing in the 1880s.
By claiming that Hemingway overstated the novel’s influence on modern American literature.
By suggesting that the qualities the critics see as flaws may serve a deliberate satirical purpose.
By arguing that Tom Sawyer’s scheme reveals Twain’s admiration for the imagination of children.

b.v: In 1846 Edgar Allan Poe published “The Philosophy of Composition,” an essay that [[purports|V02-purport]] to explain how he wrote his poem “The Raven.” Poe insists that nothing in the poem was left to chance: he claims he chose its length, its melancholy tone, and its refrain, “Nevermore,” in advance, and that the work proceeded “with the precision and rigid consequence of a mathematical problem.” Many readers have doubted that the poem was really composed so [[meticulously|V05-meticulous]]. Some suspect that Poe, who enjoyed playing tricks on his audience, described the process this way after the fact, to make a poem that may have begun more [[spontaneously|V04-spontaneously]] seem a feat of pure design.

q.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Poe presented the writing of “The Raven” as a carefully calculated process, though many readers question whether his account is accurate.
Poe wrote “The Philosophy of Composition” to answer critics who had called “The Raven” careless.
Poe admitted in a later essay that “The Raven” had been composed spontaneously.
Poe believed that writing poetry and solving mathematical problems require the same skills.

b.v: Walt Whitman revised Leaves of Grass, first published in 1855, for the rest of his life, and its longest poem, later titled “Song of Myself,” celebrates a speaker [[expansive|V10-expansive]] enough to embrace everything he encounters. That speaker treats his own inconsistency as a sign of his largeness rather than as a weakness to [[rectify|V01-rectify]]: ______

q.s: Which quotation from “Song of Myself” most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “I celebrate myself, and sing myself,”
“I loafe and invite my soul,”
“I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.”
“Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)”

b.v: Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852), a novel depicting the cruelty of slavery, sold hundreds of thousands of copies in the United States within a year of its publication. Some historians argue that the novel did more than reflect antislavery feeling that already existed in the North: it actively changed the minds of many Northern readers who had previously been indifferent to slavery.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians’ argument?
o: Stowe’s novel also sold very well in Britain, where slavery had already been abolished.
Letters and diaries from the 1850s show that many Northerners who had expressed no opinion about slavery before reading the novel described it as having turned them against slavery.
Most of the novel’s first readers in the North were already members of antislavery societies.
Several writers in the South published novels defending slavery in response to Stowe’s book.

b.v: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, but fewer than a dozen were published during her lifetime, usually without her name. After her death in 1886, her sister Lavinia found the poems locked away and helped bring them into print. The first editions, prepared in the 1890s by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, regularized Dickinson’s [[idiosyncratic|V09-idiosyncratic]] punctuation and capitalization, replacing many of her dashes and sometimes changing words to create smoother rhymes. Only in 1955 did the scholar Thomas H. Johnson publish an edition based closely on her manuscripts. Thus, readers before 1955 who knew Dickinson’s work only from the early editions ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: were likely unaware that Dickinson had written any poems during her lifetime.
read poems that Lavinia Dickinson had substantially rewritten.
encountered versions of her poems that were more [[homogenized|V12-homogenize]] in form than the ones she had written.
could not have known that Dickinson preferred rhymed poetry to unrhymed poetry.

b.v: Herman Melville dedicated Moby-Dick to the writer he admired most during the years he spent writing ______ Nathaniel Hawthorne, whom he had met at a picnic in the Berkshire Mountains of Massachusetts in 1850.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: it:
it;
it
it, and

b.v: Before the Civil War, Samuel Clemens worked as a steamboat pilot on the Mississippi River. He later ______ his pen name from a call used by riverboat crews: “mark twain” signaled a depth of two fathoms, or twelve feet—water deep enough for a steamboat to pass safely.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: takes
took
has taken
taking

b.v: Louisa May Alcott began writing Little Women in 1868 at the urging of her publisher, Thomas Niles, who wanted a book for girls; she admitted in her journal that she did not enjoy the work. ______ the novel was an immediate success, and Niles soon asked her for a second part, which was published the following year.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: Consequently,
Specifically,
Similarly,
Nevertheless,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: Edgar Allan Poe’s story “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” was published in 1841.
It is set in Paris.
Its detective, C. Auguste Dupin, solves crimes through careful reasoning.
It is often called the first modern detective story.
Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, acknowledged Poe’s influence on his own detective fiction.

q.s: The student wants to emphasize the influence of Poe’s story on later fiction. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Poe’s story “The Murders in the Rue Morgue,” published in 1841, is set in Paris.
C. Auguste Dupin, the detective in a story by Poe, solves crimes through careful reasoning.
Often called the first modern detective story, Poe’s “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1841) influenced later writers such as Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes.
Arthur Conan Doyle created the detective Sherlock Holmes.

b.v: F. Scott Fitzgerald died in 1940 believing that his career had failed. The Great Gatsby (1925) had sold far fewer copies than he had hoped, and unsold copies from its second printing were still in his publisher’s warehouse. The novel’s fortunes changed during World War II, when about 150,000 copies were printed in a special edition and distributed free to American servicemen. Read by a new generation after the war, the once-neglected book is now ______ in American high school classrooms.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[imperceptible|V11-imperceptible]]
[[sporadic|V11-sporadic]]
[[ubiquitous|V09-ubiquitous]]
[[obsolete|V02-obsolete]]

b.v: Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) received mixed reviews; the novelist Richard Wright, for one, complained that it lacked a serious message. By the time Hurston died in 1960, her books were out of print, and she was buried in an unmarked grave in Florida. In 1973 the writer Alice Walker located the grave and placed a headstone on it, and her 1975 essay “In Search of Zora Neale Hurston” was ______ in bringing Hurston’s work back to readers.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[instrumental|V02-instrumental]]
[[innocuous|V07-innocuous]]
[[superficial|V01-superficial]]
[[punctilious|V11-punctilious]]

b.v: In Death in the Afternoon (1932), Ernest Hemingway compared good prose to an iceberg: “The dignity of movement of an ice-berg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water.” A writer who knows a subject well, he argued, can leave much of it out, and readers will still sense what is missing. His story “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927) applies this principle: a man and a woman waiting for a train in Spain talk about seemingly trivial things, and the operation they are really discussing is never named. Some readers, however, find that such omissions make the story more [[opaque|V01-opaque]] than suggestive.

q.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a writer’s early failures, explains how he overcame them, and then praises one of his stories.
It presents a writer’s principle, gives an example of a work that applies it, and notes a reservation that some readers have about the approach.
It compares two of a writer’s stories, argues that one is superior, and explains why critics disagree.
It summarizes the plot of a story and then explains how critics’ views of the story changed over time.

b.v: Text 1

Robert Frost’s “The Road Not Taken” (1916) is among the most frequently quoted poems in American literature, especially at graduations. In its popular reading, the poem [[extols|V01-extol]] individualism: by taking the road “less traveled by,” the speaker chooses independence over conformity, and “that has made all the difference.”
Text 2

Many critics consider that reading [[facile|V07-facile]]. Earlier in the poem, the speaker admits that the two roads had been worn “really about the same.” And the famous final lines are set in the future—“I shall be telling this with a sigh / Somewhere ages and ages hence”—suggesting that the speaker is imagining how he will later describe a choice that, at the time, was nearly arbitrary.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the popular reading described in Text 1?
o: By arguing that the poem rejects individualism and instead praises conformity.
By claiming that the poem is rarely understood because its language is unusually difficult.
By agreeing that the speaker chose an unusual path but questioning whether the choice affected his life.
By arguing that the reading [[overlooks|V07-overlook_neglect]] details suggesting that the speaker’s choice was less distinctive than he will later claim.

b.v: Before writing The Grapes of Wrath (1939), John Steinbeck visited camps of migrant farmworkers in California as a reporter. In 1936 he published a series of articles for the San Francisco News, later collected as The Harvest Gypsies, describing families who had fled the Dust Bowl of the Great Plains only to find low wages, hunger, and hostility. The novel follows one such family, the Joads, from Oklahoma to California. Its harsh portrait of the state’s large growers drew intense [[scrutiny|V06-scrutiny]], and in 1939 the board of supervisors of Kern County, California, banned the book from local schools and libraries.

q.s: According to the text, what did Steinbeck draw on in writing The Grapes of Wrath?
o: His own childhood on a farm in Oklahoma
Interviews with growers in Kern County
His observations as a reporter visiting camps of migrant workers
Letters sent to him by readers of the San Francisco News

b.v: Langston Hughes’s short poem “Harlem” (1951) asks what becomes of a “dream deferred”: the hopes of Black Americans, postponed again and again. The poem offers a series of possible answers, each more troubling than the one before, and it ends by raising an [[ominous|V09-ominous]] possibility—that frustration, left unresolved, may turn violent: ______

q.s: Which quotation from “Harlem” most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “What happens to a dream deferred?”
“Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?”
“Maybe it just sags / like a heavy load.”
“Or does it explode?”

b.v: Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman, published in 2015, presents Scout Finch as an adult and portrays her father, Atticus, as far less admirable than the hero of To Kill a Mockingbird (1960). When the book appeared, some readers treated it as a sequel. Many scholars argue instead that Watchman was an early version of the story from which Mockingbird later grew.

q.s: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the scholars’ claim?
o: Records show that Lee submitted the manuscript of Go Set a Watchman to her editor in 1957, before she wrote To Kill a Mockingbird, and that the editor encouraged her to develop its scenes from Scout’s childhood into a new book.
Go Set a Watchman sold more than a million copies in the first week after its publication.
Many readers who admired To Kill a Mockingbird said they were disappointed by Go Set a Watchman.
To Kill a Mockingbird won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1961.

b.v: Toni Morrison’s Beloved (1987) was inspired by the case of Margaret Garner, a woman who escaped from slavery in Kentucky in 1856 and who, when slave catchers found her family in Ohio, killed her young daughter rather than see the child returned to slavery. Morrison learned of the case from a nineteenth-century newspaper article she came across while editing The Black Book (1974), a collection of documents from African American history. She later wrote that she [[deliberately|V10-deliberately]] did no further research on Garner, so that she would be free to invent her character’s inner life. Readers should therefore ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: conclude that Morrison knew little about the history of slavery when she wrote Beloved.
not treat Beloved as a historically exact account of Margaret Garner’s life.
assume that The Black Book contains Morrison’s own account of Garner’s inner life.
regard the events of Garner’s life as having been invented by Morrison.

b.v: Most of William Faulkner’s novels are set in Yoknapatawpha County, a fictional part of Mississippi modeled on the county where he lived. For Absalom, Absalom! (1936), Faulkner drew a map of this invented place and signed it with a title of his own ______ “William Faulkner, Sole Owner & Proprietor.”

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: invention;
invention
invention, which
invention:

b.v: In 1993 Toni Morrison became the first Black woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Swedish Academy, which selects the winners, ______ her as an author “who in novels characterized by visionary force and poetic import, gives life to an essential aspect of American reality.”

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: described
describe
have described
describing

b.v: Ralph Ellison’s first novel, Invisible Man (1952), won the National Book Award, and for decades readers waited for his second. Ellison worked on it for some forty years, though a fire at his summer home in Massachusetts in 1967 destroyed part of the manuscript. ______ he never finished it: a shortened version, edited by John F. Callahan and titled Juneteenth, appeared in 1999, five years after Ellison’s death.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: For example,
Similarly,
Ultimately,
By contrast,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: James Baldwin (1924–1987) was born in Harlem, New York City.
His first novel, Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953), draws on his youth as a teenage preacher.
He moved to Paris in 1948 and spent much of his later life in France.
His essay collection The Fire Next Time (1963) examines race in America.
Many readers consider his essays as important as his novels.

q.s: The student wants to introduce Baldwin to an audience unfamiliar with him, emphasizing the [[versatility|V02-versatility]] of his writing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: James Baldwin, who was born in Harlem in 1924, moved to Paris in 1948.
James Baldwin (1924–1987), an American writer born in Harlem, wrote both novels, such as Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953), and essays, such as those collected in The Fire Next Time (1963).
The Fire Next Time (1963) is an essay collection that examines race in America.
Many readers consider Baldwin’s essays as important as his novels.

b.v: Upton Sinclair spent seven weeks in 1904 working undercover in the meatpacking plants of Chicago, and his novel The Jungle (1906) was meant to [[expose|V04-expose]] the misery of the immigrant workers he met there. Readers, however, were most horrified by its descriptions of spoiled and contaminated meat. The public outcry ______ the passage of two federal laws that same year, the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. “I aimed at the public’s heart,” Sinclair later wrote, “and by accident I hit it in the stomach.”

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[precipitated|V03-precipitate]]
[[mitigated|V07-mitigate]]
[[repudiated|V01-repudiate]]
[[obviated|V08-obviate]]

b.v: In Washington Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle” (1819), Rip wanders into the Catskill Mountains, drinks liquor with a band of strange men, and falls asleep for twenty years, missing the entire American Revolution. When he returns to his village, he does not realize that the colonies have become an independent nation, and when he calls himself a loyal subject of King George III, he ______ provokes an angry uproar among the townspeople.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
o: [[deliberately|V10-deliberately]]
[[scrupulously|V05-scrupulously]]
[[inadvertently|V07-inadvertently]]
[[surreptitiously|V11-surreptitiously]]

b.v: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie (1944) a “memory play”: its events are presented as its narrator, Tom Wingfield, remembers them, and Williams asked for music and lighting that would make the stage look openly unrealistic. The play begins with Tom stepping forward to address the audience. ⟦“I have tricks in my pocket, I have things up my sleeve,” he says. “But I am the opposite of a stage magician. He gives you illusion that has the appearance of truth. I give you truth in the pleasant disguise of illusion.”⟧

q.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
o: It reveals that Tom intends to deceive the audience about the events of his past.
It explains why Williams later rejected the term “memory play.”
It contrasts Tom’s former career as a magician with his later work as a writer.
It establishes that the play will convey truth through a form that openly acknowledges its own [[artifice|V10-artifice]].

b.v: Text 1

Ray Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451 (1953) imagines a future in which “firemen” burn books, and it is often taught as a warning about government censorship. Its hero, the fireman Guy Montag, begins secretly saving the books he is ordered to destroy and is eventually hunted by the state.
Text 2

Bradbury himself grew impatient with that reading. In later interviews he insisted that the novel was less about censorship than about how television and other mass entertainment erode people’s interest in reading. The text supports him: Montag’s fire chief, Captain Beatty, explains that the burning of books “didn’t come from the Government down.” People had stopped reading on their own, Beatty says, long before the firemen began their work.

q.s: Based on the texts, how would Bradbury (Text 2) most likely respond to the reading described in Text 1?
o: He would argue that Montag is not the true hero of the novel.
He would consider the reading [[reductive|V07-reductive]], since it overlooks the novel’s concern with how people abandoned books before the state began to burn them.
He would agree that government censorship is the novel’s main subject but object to how the book is taught.
He would claim that the novel was written to predict the invention of television.

b.v: Gwendolyn Brooks grew up in Bronzeville, a Black neighborhood on Chicago’s South Side, and her first book of poems, A Street in Bronzeville (1945), drew its characters from the people around her. In 1950 she became the first Black author to win a Pulitzer Prize, for her second collection, Annie Allen. Though she became a [[luminary|V03-luminary]] of American poetry, Brooks never left the neighborhood behind: for decades she led poetry workshops for young people in Chicago, and in 1968 she was named Poet Laureate of Illinois, a post she held until her death in 2000.

q.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Brooks’s first book of poems was more successful than her second.
Brooks moved away from Chicago after winning the Pulitzer Prize.
Brooks achieved national recognition as a poet while remaining closely tied to the Chicago community that shaped her work.
Brooks was the first poet to be named Poet Laureate of Illinois.

b.v: In Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman (1949), Linda Loman defends her husband, Willy, an aging and unsuccessful salesman, to their sons. She insists that Willy deserves compassion because of his suffering, even though he has achieved nothing remarkable: ______

q.s: Which quotation from Linda’s speech most effectively illustrates the claim?
o: “Willy Loman never made a lot of money. His name was never in the paper.”
“He’s not the finest character that ever lived. But he’s a human being, and a terrible thing is happening to him.”
“So attention must be paid.”
“He’s not to be allowed to fall into his grave like an old dog.”

rows: Long Day’s Journey into Night (Eugene O’Neill)
A Raisin in the Sun (Lorraine Hansberry)

b.v: Eugene O’Neill finished Long Day’s Journey into Night, a painful portrait of his own family, in the early 1940s, but he asked that it not be published until twenty-five years after his death. After he died in 1953, his widow allowed it to be published and staged anyway. The play’s later history shows that a playwright could be honored for a work he never saw performed: ______

q.s: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
o: Long Day’s Journey into Night premiered on Broadway in 1956 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1957.
Death of a Salesman premiered on Broadway in 1949 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama that same year.
A Raisin in the Sun premiered on Broadway in 1959 but did not win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
A Streetcar Named Desire won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1948, a year after its Broadway premiere.

b.v: During World War II, the American soldier Kurt Vonnegut was held as a prisoner of war in Dresden, Germany. He survived the Allied firebombing of the city in February 1945 by sheltering in an underground meat locker of a slaughterhouse, and he spent more than twenty years trying to write about the experience. The novel he finally published, Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), abandons conventional chronology: its hero, Billy Pilgrim, has “come unstuck in time” and moves [[intermittently|V09-intermittently]] between the war and other moments of his life. The narrator explains that the book is “short and jumbled and jangled” because “there is nothing intelligent to say about a massacre.” This explanation suggests that the novel’s fragmented structure ______

q.s: Which choice most logically completes the text?
o: was imposed on Vonnegut by an editor who wanted a shorter book.
reflects Billy Pilgrim’s belief that the bombing never took place.
was meant to make the events of the war easier for readers to follow.
is in part a response to the difficulty of describing the bombing in a conventional narrative.

b.v: Our Town (1938), Thornton Wilder’s play about daily life in the fictional village of Grover’s Corners, New ______ is performed on a nearly bare stage, with a narrator called the Stage Manager who speaks directly to the audience.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: Hampshire,
Hampshire
Hampshire;
Hampshire—

b.v: In 1897 the young Jack London joined the rush of prospectors to the Klondike region of Canada’s Yukon Territory, where gold had been discovered the year before. He found almost no gold, but the ______ hardships he witnessed there became material for his novel The Call of the Wild (1903), about a dog forced to pull sleds across the frozen north.

q.s: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
o: prospectors
prospector’s
prospectors’
prospectors’s

b.v: Edith Wharton was born in 1862 into one of the wealthy old families of New York society, the world she would later portray in The Age of Innocence (1920). ______ her depiction of that society’s rigid rules, from its formal dinners to its quiet punishment of anyone who broke them, draws on close personal observation. The novel won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize, making Wharton the first woman to receive the award for fiction.

q.s: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
o: Nevertheless,
Thus,
By contrast,
For instance,

b.v: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

v: Phillis Wheatley was born in West Africa around 1753 and brought to Boston as an enslaved child in 1761.
She began writing poetry as a teenager.
Many people at the time doubted that an enslaved African woman could write poetry.
A group of prominent Boston men examined her and signed a statement confirming that she had written her poems.

q.s: The student wants to emphasize the obstacles Wheatley faced in getting her poetry published. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: Phillis Wheatley, who was born in West Africa around 1753, began writing poetry as a teenager.
Wheatley’s book Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral was published in London in 1773.
Phillis Wheatley was brought to Boston as an enslaved child in 1761.

Because many doubted that an enslaved African woman could write poetry, Wheatley had to be examined by prominent Boston men who [[attested|V02-attest]] to her authorship, and she published her book in London after failing to find a publisher in Boston.
